pool.q: The graph of the function \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3\) is shown below. Determine the sum of the x-intercepts.
pool.sol: The x-intercepts of a function are the values of x for which \(f(x) = 0\). For the quadratic function \(f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3\), we can find the x-intercepts by solving the equation \(x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0\). This is a quadratic equation that can be factored. We are looking for two numbers that multiply to 3 and add to -4. These numbers are -1 and -3. Therefore, the equation can be factored as \((x-1)(x-3) = 0\). The solutions are \(x=1\) and \(x=3\). These are the x-intercepts. The sum of the x-intercepts is \(1 + 3 = 4\). Alternatively, for a quadratic equation of the form \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), the sum of the roots (which correspond to the x-intercepts when \(f(x) = 0\)) is given by \(-\frac{b}{a}\). In this case, \(a=1\) and \(b=-4\), so the sum of the x-intercepts is \(-\frac{-4}{1} = 4\). [M1] [A1]

pool.topic: Paper 3 Extended Investigation: Roots of Unity, Chebyshev Polynomials & Product of Chords
pool.q:
[AA HL Paper 3 Extended Investigation — 27 marks]
Let \(\omega = e^{i\frac{2\pi}{n}}\) be the primitive \(n\)-th root of unity for \(n \ge 2\), and consider the polynomial \(P_n(z) = z^n - 1\).
(a) Write down all roots of \(P_n(z) = 0\) in terms of \(\omega\) and explain why \(1 + z + z^2 + \dots + z^{n-1} = \prod_{k=1}^{n-1} (z - \omega^k)\). [5]
(b) By substituting \(z = 1\) into the identity in part (a), show that \(\prod_{k=1}^{n-1} |1 - \omega^k| = n\). Interpret this result geometrically in terms of the lengths of the chords drawn from vertex \(A_0(1, 0)\) to the remaining \(n-1\) vertices of a regular \(n\)-gon inscribed in the unit circle. [7]
(c) Show that \(|1 - e^{i\theta}| = 2\left|\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|\) for any \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). [4]
(d) Hence prove the trigonometric product identity:
\[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)\cdot s\sin\left(\frac{(n-1)\pi}{n}\right) = \frac{n}{2^{n-1}}\] [6]
(e) Verify the identity in part (d) directly for \(n = 3\), \(n = 4\), and \(n = 6\), and find the exact value of \(\prod_{k=1}^{11} \sin\left(\frac{k\pi}{12}\right)\). [5]
pool.ans: (a) Roots 1, ω, ..., ω^(n-1); (b) Product of (n-1) chord lengths from (1,0) equals n; (d) n / 2^(n-1); (e) For n=12: 12 / 2¹¹ = 3 / 512

Geometrically, \(|1 - \omega^k|\) is the Euclidean chord length from \((1,0)\) to \(\omega^k\), so the product of all \(n-1\) diagonals/sides from one vertex of a unit regular \(n\)-gon equals \(n\) [R1] [A1] [A1]
